extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent prosecutors, and applicants before the EPO/PCT
extracted.subtask_description: A concise summary of the 2024 updates to the European Patent Office Guidelines for Examination (effective 1 March 2024), highlighting substantive changes to examination practice (priority entitlement, plausibility/inventive step, evidence evaluation), disclosure/enabling requirements for AI and antibodies, sequence listing rules, opposition acceleration, and other procedural amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and structure of the EPO/PCT Guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: The Guidelines give instructions on the practices and procedures to be followed in the examination of European and international applications and patents in accordance with the EPC, the PCT and their Implementing Regulations. The PCT-EPO Guidelines follow the same structure as the EPC Guidelines (minus Part D) and are adapted to PCT specifics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Guidelines as the authoritative manual on EPO and PCT-EPO examination practice; consult the corresponding parts for EPC vs PCT specifics (PCT has no opposition/limitation/revocation procedures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Entitlement to priority — rebuttable presumption and burden shift (G 1/22 & G 2/22)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Absent any substantiated indication to the contrary, there is a strong rebuttable presumption under the EPC that an applicant or joint applicants claiming priority ... are also entitled to the claimed priority. The burden of proof is shifted, and the examining division, opponent or third party challenging an applicant’s entitlement to priority has to prove that this entitlement is missing." (Part A-III-6.1, as amended.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joint filing (including the priority applicant) typically implies an agreement allowing all of them to rely on the priority right unless substantial facts indicate otherwise. The EPC does not set formal requirements for transfer of the priority right; prior formalistic practices are loosened (see G 1/22 and G 2/22).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility: reliance on newly submitted effects for inventive step (G 2/21)
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is also possible to rely on new effects submitted subsequently during the proceedings by the applicant, provided the skilled person, having the common general knowledge at the effective filing date in mind, and based on the application as originally filed, would derive said effect as being encompassed by the technical teaching and embodied by the same originally disclosed invention." (Part G-VII, 5.2)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants may submit new technical effects during prosecution, but those effects are only admissible for inventive-step assessment if the skilled person would derive them from the original disclosure with the common general knowledge. The Guidelines incorporate the EBA's plausibility approach but leave scope for interpretation in future Board decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free evaluation of evidence — treatment of post‑published evidence (G 2/21 and E-IV-4)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Any evidence submitted to prove a technical effect that can be taken into account for the assessment of inventive step is assessed in accordance with the principle of free evaluation of evidence... Such evidence may not be disregarded solely on the ground that it is post-published (G 2/21)." (Part G-VII, 11) and detailed in Part E-IV, 4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The competent department must assess whether alleged facts are sufficiently established based on all submissions; there are no rigid rules about which types of evidence are convincing. Evaluation must be comprehensive, reasoned, and bound by logic and probability. Admissibly submitted evidence (including post‑published evidence) cannot be disregarded as a matter of principle; the department must explain its reasoning in the decision and weigh arguments for and against to the required standard of proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure/enabling requirements for AI and mathematical-methods inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: "Occasionally applications are filed in which there is a fundamental insufficiency ... another example can be found in the field of artificial intelligence if the mathematical methods and the training datasets are disclosed in insufficient detail to reproduce the technical effect over the whole range claimed. Such a lack of detail may result in a disclosure that is more like an invitation to a research programme." (Part F-III-3) and "If the technical effect is dependent on particular characteristics of the training dataset used, those characteristics that are required to reproduce the technical effect must be disclosed unless the skilled person can determine them without undue burden ... However, in general, there is no need to disclose the specific training dataset itself." (Part G-II-3.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AI-related applications require disclosure akin to biotech: mathematical methods and the essential characteristics of training data must be described sufficiently to reproduce the claimed technical effect across the claimed range; mere allegations of effect are insufficient though exhaustive proof is not required. Do not assume that omitting dataset characteristics will be acceptable where those characteristics are necessary to reproduce the effect. Also: the EPO checks that the designated inventor is a natural person (J 8/20/DABUS case law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Antibody claims — permissible definitions and use of epitopes (G-II-6.1, 6.1.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Antibodies may be defined by their target antigen and other functional features (binding affinity, neutralising properties, induction of apoptosis, internalisation, inhibition/activation of receptors). Claims by reference to epitope are discussed: an antibody may be claimed by reference to its epitope, but some passages relating to epitope definitions have been reformulated/deleted in certain sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that define antibodies only by competition with a reference antibody disclosed for the first time in the application will normally not sufficiently identify antibodies for search and may trigger an invitation under Rule 63(1) to indicate subject-matter for search. Where there is no indication to the contrary, assume a prior‑art antibody binding the same antigen will have the claimed functional properties (burden of proof on the applicant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Antibody enablement and claim scope — requirement to enable production and verification
rubrics_metrics.description: "The application must enable the person skilled in the art to produce further antibodies having the claimed functional property without undue burden ... the functional definition must allow the skilled person to easily and unambiguously verify whether they are working inside or outside the scope of the claim. The claim should therefore normally include the relevant characteristics of the method used to determine and define the functional property." (Part G-II, 6.1.3)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional antibody claims must include or enable the characteristics and methods needed to determine the functional property so that skilled persons can reproduce and verify the claimed property without undue burden; otherwise sufficiency objections (Article 83-like) and search/inventive-step problems may follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antibody inventive-step standard — surprising technical effect or lack of reasonable expectation of success (G-II-6.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The subject‑matter of a claim defining a novel antibody binding to a known antigen does not involve an inventive step unless a surprising technical effect is shown ... or unless there was no reasonable expectation of success of obtaining antibodies having the required properties ... Inventive step is not acknowledged solely on the basis that an antibody is structurally different from the prior‑art antibodies. ... Nevertheless, antibodies can be inventive if the application overcomes technical difficulties in generating or manufacturing the claimed antibodies. A novel type of functional antibody format may also be considered inventive." (Part G-II-6.2)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish inventive step for antibodies, show an unexpected improvement or property over prior art or demonstrate that obtaining antibodies with the required properties was not reasonably expected; structural unpredictability alone is insufficient. Evidence of overcoming technical difficulties or a novel functional format can support inventiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: ST.26 sequence listings and divisional applications (A-IV-5 and A-III, 13.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nucleotide and amino acid sequences must be represented in a sequence listing complying with WIPO Standard ST.26. Where the parent application's listing is ST.25, it must be converted to ST.26 for divisionals filed on/after 1 July 2022, and applicants may file the parent application's ST.25 listing in PDF as part of the divisional to avoid risk of adding/deleting subject‑matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing the ST.25 listing in PDF as part of the divisional can avoid conversion-subject-matter risks and, by EPO practice, those pages are excluded from the calculation of additional 'page fees' if the XML ST.26 listing is also filed. Follow WIPO ST.26 Annex VII recommendations to prevent added/deleted subject matter during conversion. Certified copy rules and page-count exceptions (e.g., for Form 1001 and ST.25 pages) are specified and must be observed to avoid extra fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceleration/priority treatment of opposition proceedings when UPC or national infringement actions pending (D-VIII-1.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Oppositions are to be given priority if a party to the proceedings has submitted a reasoned request for accelerated processing in a case where an infringement action in respect of the European patent is pending before the Unified Patent Court or a national court ... or if the EPO is informed by the UPC, a national court or competent authority that infringement actions are pending." (Part D-VIII-1.2)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties can request accelerated opposition processing where related infringement litigation is pending; the EPO may also accelerate on notice from courts/authorities. File well‑reasoned requests and notify the EPO of parallel litigation to seek priority treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation of the description / Article 84 examination (D-V-5)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The description of the patent may be examined for compliance with the requirements of Art. 84 only when, and then only to the extent that, an amendment of the patent introduces non-compliance with Art. 84. In particular, inconsistencies between the description and the claims resulting from amendments during opposition proceedings and casting doubt on the subject-matter for which protection is sought must be avoided." (Part D-V-5)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPO will not re-examine the description under Art.84 unless an amendment causes non-compliance. When amending claims, ensure the description is consistent with allowed claims to avoid objection and doubt on the scope of protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolition of the notification fiction / impact on time limit computations (D-VII-4.3; Rule 131(2) EPC)
rubrics_metrics.description: A major amendment relates to the abolition of the notification fiction (the '10‑days rule') that assumed documents sent by the EPO were received by the addressee on the 10th day after posting; this affects computation of time limits. Amendments have also been made regarding receipt of EPO notifications by postal services (Parts E-II, 2.3 and II, 2.4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must revise calendaring and time-limit computations in light of the abolished notification fiction. Check the updated rules for service/receipt timing, especially where postal services are involved, to avoid missed deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection inventions and deletion/amendment of other substantive sections (G-VI,7 and deletion of G-VI,4)
rubrics_metrics.description: New Part G-VI, 7 relating to selection inventions has been largely amended; the previous section on enablement of a prior‑art document (G-VI, 4) has been deleted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult the amended selection inventions section for updated tests and practice; note deletion of prior-art-document enablement guidance and adjust examination/response strategies accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural and administrative updates (validation states, UPCA/unitary effect, forms, representation, refunds, plain language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments include adding Georgia as a validation state (A-III,12.1), additions relating to the Unified Patent Court/unitary patent (General Part 8; Part C-V,2.1), new sections on form of documents (A-VIII,2) and signatures (A-VIII,3), representation before the EPO as ISA or SISA (Part B II,6), a new subsection on refund of the appeal fee (A-X 10.2.6), and an initiative to harmonise/modernise language (plain language and gender-neutral terms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Update filing/checklist practices to reflect new validation states and unitary-patent guidance; ensure forms and signatures comply with new sections; check representation rules for ISA/SISA roles; be aware of refund procedures and the EPO's plain-language wording changes.
